source: Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models (arXiv 2601.00514)
finding: Mid-reasoning shifts (an LLM 'aha') are rare, do not grow with RL training, and mostly go with lower accuracy.
numbers: Over 11M traces; Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B and Llama3.1-8B under GRPO. Shifts in 6.31% of traces; formal Aha events 1.79%. Pooled accuracy with a shift 6.6% vs 29.0% without. Qwen-1.5B: 2.57% vs 16.44% (N=723,200). DeepSeek-R1 shifts 0.40-0.60%, GPT-4o 2.20-3.00%.
quote: reasoning shifts are rare, do not become more frequent with training, and seldom improve accuracy
limits: Three domains with checkable answers (cryptic crosswords, MATH-500, Rush Hour). Shift detection uses lexical cues and plan change. Small open models.
agent_relevance: Do not treat a spontaneous 'wait, actually' in a trace as evidence of a working impasse break (S6 to O6). The shift is a symptom of trouble, not a fix.

source: Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models: shifts by domain
finding: Shift rate depends on task: puzzles with state search show many more shifts than crosswords.
numbers: Xwords 1.22%, Math 2.65%, Rush Hour 14.32%. Qwen-7B Math 1.50%, Llama-8B Math 5.04%. Math with shifts: -18.35 pp accuracy (temperature analysis); -22.88 pp in low-entropy traces, -7.40 pp in high-entropy traces.
limits: Correlational. Shifts rise when the model is already stuck.
agent_relevance: A shift trigger should be conditioned on measured uncertainty, not on the model's own words.

source: Illusion of Insight: forced reconsideration intervention
finding: Making the model reconsider helps most when token entropy is high; it barely helps on other tasks.
numbers: Math pass 1 to pass 2: 32.21% to 40.62% (+8.41 pp); 50,574 wrong-to-right vs 23,500 right-to-wrong. Xwords +0.45 pp. Rush Hour +0.01 pp. Gains larger on top-20% entropy items. Judge kappa 0.726 (0.79 vs human majority).
limits: Prompt-level intervention. Does not prove an internal mechanism. Gain only in Math.
agent_relevance: Supports gating O6 on an uncertainty signal (high entropy or failed S8 check) rather than always restructuring.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing reasoning capability via RL
finding: The famous 'aha moment' of R1-Zero: a rise in the word 'wait' and self-reflection during RL training, alongside better AIME scores.
numbers: AIME 2024 pass@1 rose from 15.6% to 77.9% during RL training. 'Aha moment' defined as a sudden increase in use of the word 'wait'. Paper itself cites a blog titled 'There may not be aha moment in r1-zero-like training'.
quote: Wait, wait. Wait. That's an aha moment I can flag here.
limits: Anecdote from one intermediate checkpoint plus a word-frequency curve. No causal test that the aha behaviour caused the gain.
agent_relevance: The AI 'aha' claim is lexical. Our agent should log real state changes (new representation), not the word 'wait'.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Aha Moment Revisited: Are VLMs Truly Capable of Self Verification in Inference-time Scaling?
finding: In RL-tuned vision-language models, aha moments are uncommon and add little; self-verification is weak and majority vote beats it.
numbers: Aha moments in 8.3% of responses (Qwen-based models, GeoQA170K and MathVista); correction probability low. Majority vote gains +4.5% over greedy; best-of-N with self-verification gave limited gain or drops up to -16.7% (VLAA models).
quote: A-ha moments occur in fewer than 10% of cases, and even when manually selected, yield only marginal
limits: Small Qwen2-VL-family models on geometry. Verification done by the same model.
agent_relevance: The verification stage (S8) should not be the same model re-reading its own answer. Prefer independent samples and voting.

source: Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (nazonazo) benchmark (arXiv 2509.14704)
finding: Insight-style riddles stay hard for LLMs without retrieval; reasoning models do better, but a main failure is rejecting a correct idea.
numbers: 201 riddles; human reference n=126 on 120 items, mean 52.9% (95% CI 46.6-59.2). 38 LLMs zero-shot: non-reasoning 7.6%, reasoning 17.6% on the 120 subset. Full 201: reasoning 19.25% vs non-reasoning 9.42%, OR 2.29 (1.99-2.64). GPT-5 inside human CI. Parameter count did not predict accuracy; release date did.
limits: Japanese-language riddles; no formal LLM-vs-human tests; contamination controlled by retrieval-free protocol.
agent_relevance: Generation of the right idea is not the only bottleneck; commitment is. S8 must decide when to accept.

source: Nazonazo: verification failure measure
finding: Models write down the correct answer during search, then do not endorse it and answer wrongly (verification failure).
numbers: Verification failures were 5.23% to 39.34% of each model's wrong answers (Gemini 2.5 Flash lowest, Grok 4 highest). Reasoning-inclusive few-shot demos raised accuracy in all 4 tested models, significantly in 2.
limits: Four models with usable thought logs. Analogy to feelings of rightness is loose.
agent_relevance: Add an explicit 'candidate seen and later dropped' check to S8: re-score earlier candidates before the final answer.

source: Nazonazo: language of the thought log
finding: Thinking in Japanese versus English did not reliably help.
limits: Language choice was not randomised; the model picked it.
agent_relevance: Reasoning language is a weak lever; do not build a language-switch operator.

source: Frontiers in AI (2023) ChatGPT on verbal insight problems (PMC10244637)
finding: ChatGPT (Jan 2023) scored about like the typical human on 30 verbal insight problems.
numbers: 30 problems (Ansburg and Dominowski 2000), 15 practice and 15 transfer. ChatGPT 7/15 and 5/15 (12/30). Humans n=20: median 0.55 practice, 0.35 transfer.
quote: The global performance of ChatGPT equalled the most probable outcome for the human sample
limits: Tiny human sample; one model version; verbal problems only; feedback and strategic hints were given after failures. Public puzzles, so contamination is possible.
agent_relevance: Hints after failure (control, then strategic instructions) resemble a scaffold; their effect was not isolated.

source: SPLAT: Weak-eval-Strong, situation puzzles (arXiv 2410.06733)
finding: Lateral-thinking situation puzzles are hard for LLMs; training or prompting on the benchmark's reasoning data lifts other lateral sets a little.
numbers: 975 puzzles. Avg accuracy: GPT-4 41.70%, WizardLM-2 35.45%, Llama3-70B 34.50%, GPT-4 Turbo 32.91%, Llama3-8B 17.05%. BrainTeaser Word: Llama3-70B 71.20 to 79.54; Llama3-8B 46.20 to 58.07. RiddleSense GPT-4 88.83 to 89.23.
limits: Single run, 15-round cap; judge model is also a contender.
agent_relevance: Transfer is large for weak models and tiny for strong ones.

source: McCoy (2025) Creativity or Brute Force? Brainteasers as a window (arXiv 2505.10844)
finding: LLMs often find the short insightful solution to brainteasers, but sometimes still use brute force when a clever route exists.
numbers: Abstract only: five stages probed (parsing, solution generation, self-correction, sketches, hints). No numbers read.
limits: Only the abstract was read; numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: Test whether our agent picks the short route; log solution length as an insight proxy.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER lateral thinking puzzles (arXiv 2310.05057)
finding: Large human-model gap on lateral puzzles, wider when models are tested for consistency across rewritten forms.
numbers: 1,100 puzzles. Abstract gives no accuracy numbers.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Consistency across rewrites is a better test of understanding than single accuracy.

source: Danek & Wiley (2017) What about false insights? Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Strong Aha! ratings also occur on wrong solutions, so a felt aha is not a reliable sign of a correct answer.
numbers: 70 students, 37 magic tricks, 1,778 attempts: 36.8% correct, 63.2% wrong. Aha rating correct 66.50 vs wrong 52.34, t(69)=10.21. 417 of 1,124 wrong solutions (37%) scored above the correct mean (false insights). Certainty 70.55 vs 56.14.
limits: No feedback given; Aha prompt mentioned suddenness and certainty; magic tricks only; correlational.
agent_relevance: A model's confident 'I see it' feeling must not stand in for S8 verification.

source: Danek & Wiley (2017): predictors of Aha
finding: Aha has parts: pleasure, suddenness, certainty. Relief goes with correct answers, surprise with wrong ones.
numbers: Correct (N=654): pleasure beta 0.35, suddenness 0.24, certainty 0.20, relief 0.09. Wrong (N=1,124): pleasure 0.38, certainty 0.27, suddenness 0.16, surprise 0.09. Correct solutions faster: 35.81 s vs 42.46 s.
limits: Same limits as above.
agent_relevance: Surprise on arrival might flag a false insight; a cheap tag for the agent log.

source: Danek & Wiley (2020) What causes the insight memory advantage? Cognition 205
finding: Solutions found with Aha are remembered a week later better, but the cause is correctness, certainty and pleasure, not sudden restructuring.
numbers: Exp 1 (magic tricks, 738 generated solutions): Aha correct 65.66 vs wrong 51.28, d=0.52; Aha-recall link d=0.51 (replicates Danek 2013). One week later 57.7% of correct vs 35.4% of wrong solutions recalled. Exp 2: sudden-restructuring measure did not predict recall.
quote: However, it did not seem to rely on having reached the solution via a sudden restructuring process.
limits: Magic trick videos; restructuring measured by verb ratings, a proxy; Exp 2 second session online.
agent_relevance: Store solutions that passed S8 with high certainty; do not rank memory by how sudden the change was.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem. Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Insight is about the solver's experience, not the problem type; Aha tracks accuracy within insight problems but barely within non-insight ones.
numbers: Exp1 N=184 after exclusions, Exp1a 74, Exp2 117. Accuracy classic insight 0.51/0.49/0.45; non-insight 0.54/0.64/0.56; CRA 0.37/0.45/0.47. Aha-accuracy r: insight 0.50/0.40/0.495; non-insight 0.02/0.24/0.19. Impasse and surprise lowered accuracy; pleasure raised it.
limits: Students at one university; text and Table 1 disagree for Exp1a; results not stable across experiments; Aha self-report after solving.
agent_relevance: Problem labels like 'insight problem' do not predict who needs O6. Trigger by observed stall instead.

source: Gilhooly (2016) Incubation and intuition in creative problem solving, Frontiers in Psychology (PMC4956660)
finding: Incubation effect is real but small; best-supported account is unconscious work; conscious rehearsal during the break is largely ruled out.
numbers: Sio and Ormerod 2009 meta-analysis: 117 studies, mean d=0.29. Strick et al. 2011: 92 decision studies, g=0.224. Eight tests of intermittent work averaged r=0.11.
limits: Review by one author; no failed replications reported in the text read.
agent_relevance: A pause plus a low-demand side task is a cheap candidate for O6; effect size is small, so do not expect much.

source: Gilhooly (2016): moderators of incubation
finding: Benefit is larger with an undemanding task during the break; immediate versus delayed incubation depends on task.
numbers: Sio and Ormerod: undemanding interpolated task beats demanding task or rest. Strick: larger with more options, shorter presentation, shorter incubation. Gilhooly 2012: immediate incubation helped divergent tasks more; Nordgren 2011: delay helped decisions more.
limits: Moderator findings from different literatures; mixed.
agent_relevance: In an LLM, a 'break' could be a context reset or unrelated sub-task; test it, do not assume it.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? Psychological Bulletin 135, 94-120
finding: Overall positive incubation effect; bigger for divergent thinking than for linguistic or visual insight problems. Longer preparation gives a bigger effect.
numbers: 117 studies (count from Gilhooly 2016; the abstract has no numbers). Low-demand task during break beat rest for linguistic insight problems; high-demand task shrank the effect.
limits: Abstract read; effect-size tables not opened. Authors caution against practical use.
agent_relevance: Prepare longer before pausing: attempt first, then switch.

source: Weisberg (2015) Toward an integrated theory of insight, Thinking & Reasoning 21:5-39 (via secondary snippet)
finding: Weisberg's view: insight rests on ordinary conscious processes, with restructuring as the marker. Impasse is not required.
numbers: A later study (N=42, 70 word puzzles) found impasse not a prerequisite; restructuring more often preceded insight solutions but also appeared in non-insight ones. Taken from a search snippet.
limits: Not opened; paper itself not read.
agent_relevance: Argues against building S6 as a mandatory gate; use impasse as one trigger among several.

source: Wallas (1926) The Art of Thought: preparation, incubation, illumination, verification
finding: Origin of the four-stage model; descriptive, from introspection, not tested experimentally.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened. Gilhooly 2016 says famous anecdotes (Coleridge, Mozart, Kekule) are described as proven false.
agent_relevance: The four stages map onto S-states, but the evidence base is anecdote; the schema should not lean on them.

source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving, Memory & Cognition
finding: Warmth ratings rose smoothly for algebra problems but stayed low until the solution on insight problems: solvers could not foresee the solution.
numbers: Numbers not verified this session.
limits: Not opened (recalled from memory). Later work finds mixed results.
agent_relevance: Do not use self-reported progress to detect nearness to a solution.

source: Schooler, Ohlsson & Brooks (1993) Thoughts beyond words, J Exp Psych: General
finding: Asking people to talk through insight problems while solving lowered success versus silence; verbalisation did not hurt non-insight problems.
numbers: Numbers not verified this session.
limits: Not opened (recalled from memory). Verbal overshadowing has had replication problems in other domains.
agent_relevance: Forcing a long chain of thought at an impasse might hurt; test a short-trace arm.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Matchstick arithmetic: problems needing relaxation of tighter constraints or breaking tight chunks took longer; supports representational change theory.
numbers: Numbers not verified this session.
limits: Not opened (recalled from memory). Rival is progress-monitoring theory (MacGregor et al. 2001).
agent_relevance: Gives concrete O6 moves: relax a constraint, decompose a chunk.

source: MacGregor, Ormerod & Chronicle (2001) Information processing and insight: nine-dot problem
finding: Rival to the special-process view: nine-dot difficulty fits hill-climbing with progress monitoring and lookahead.
numbers: Numbers not verified this session.
limits: Not opened; described in a search snippet only.
agent_relevance: A discriminating test: does a lookahead hint or a constraint hint help more. Both are cheap operators for us.

source: Becker, Kuhn & Sommer (2021) Verbal insight revisited (via search snippet)
finding: Neurocognitive processes differ for solutions with Aha with or without prior restructuring.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Search snippet only.
agent_relevance: Supports separating restructuring from the Aha feeling in logs.

source: Kizilirmak et al. (2019, Frontiers in Psychology): generation vs Aha in memory (via snippet)
finding: Both Aha and generated solutions linked to positive emotion; only generation predicted later memory.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Search snippet only; conflicts with a purely Aha-specific memory advantage.
agent_relevance: Self-generated beats shown; store the agent's own derived solutions with their derivation.
